title: A Feast for All Peoples and Death Swallowed Up
summary: The prophet praises the LORD for his faithful plans, for bringing down the fortified city of the ruthless, and for being a refuge to the poor and needy. On Mount Zion the LORD will prepare a rich banquet for all peoples, swallow up death forever, and wipe away tears from every face, and his people will say that this is the God they waited for. Proud Moab, by contrast, will be trampled down.
story: Chapter 24 ended with the LORD reigning on Mount Zion after judging the earth. Chapter 25 shows what that reign looks like, and it is a feast. The same mountain where the kings of the earth are humbled becomes the place where all nations eat together at God's table. This is one of the widest windows in the Old Testament onto God's purpose for the nations: not only Israel but "all the peoples" are invited, and the enemy removed is not a nation but death itself. The chapter's closing lines on Moab bring the vision back to earth, and chapter 26 continues with the song the redeemed will sing.
historical:
Like the rest of chapters 24 to 27, this chapter names no king or date, and its setting is tied to the wider debate over the section. Those who hold that Isaiah wrote it in the late eighth or early seventh century BC point to its close links with Isaiah's earlier promise that the nations would stream to the mountain of the LORD (2:2-4). Those who date the section after the exile see the ruined city of verse 2 as a city of the Persian or early Hellenistic world. As in chapter 24, the city is not named, and the praise is for a pattern of God's action as much as for a single event.

Moab, the kingdom east of the Dead Sea, receives a brief oracle in verses 10 to 12. Moab and Israel were related peoples (Genesis 19:37) and long rivals. Isaiah had already given two chapters to Moab (chapters 15 and 16), and here it becomes the example of the proud nation that refuses the feast. Its high-walled fortresses on the plateau east of the Jordan were famous for their strength, which gives verse 12 its point.
cultural:
A royal banquet was one of the great public acts of an ancient king. When a king won a victory or dedicated a palace, he fed his officials, his army, and sometimes whole populations, and the size of the feast displayed the size of his power and generosity. Assyrian kings recorded such feasts in their inscriptions. The LORD's banquet here is described in the best terms an Israelite knew: rich food full of marrow and aged wine that had been left on its sediment to develop flavor, then refined. The poor rarely ate meat at all, so a feast of choice meat was a picture of abundance beyond ordinary life.

The "shroud that enfolds all peoples" (verse 7) is probably the covering worn in mourning, when people veiled their faces or covered their heads in grief (compare 2 Samuel 15:30). Death was pictured in Canaanite myth as a god with an enormous appetite who swallowed his victims; in the Ugaritic texts from the late second millennium BC the god Mot (whose name means death) has a mouth that reaches from earth to sky. Isaiah reverses the image. The LORD is the one who swallows, and what he swallows is death.
literary: The chapter mixes two forms. Verses 1 to 5 and 9 are songs of thanksgiving, individual in verse 1 ("O LORD, You are my God") and communal in verse 9 ("we have waited for Him"). Verses 6 to 8 and 10 to 12 are prophecy. The phrase "on this mountain" ties the prophecy together, repeated in verses 6, 7, and 10. The verb swallow appears twice in verses 7 and 8 and forms the hinge of the chapter: the covering over the nations is swallowed, then death itself. Verse 8 ends with a formula of authority, "For the LORD has spoken," which marks the promise as certain. The closing image of Moab in verses 10 to 12 is deliberately undignified, a swimmer thrashing in a dung heap, the reverse of the guests at the feast.

outline.t: Praise for the LORD's faithful plans and his refuge for the poor
The banquet on the mountain and death swallowed up
The song of those who waited for the LORD

doctrines.note: Salvation here is the removal of death, grief, and disgrace, a rescue of the whole person and the whole people. The redeemed confess that they waited for God and he saved them; salvation is his act, received with joy.

The feast is for "all the peoples" and "all nations" (verses 6 and 7). God's purpose in choosing Zion was always to bless the world, a thread that runs from his promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3) to this banquet.

The chapter gives the Old Testament's clearest promise that death itself will be undone. Hope in Scripture is not merely survival after death but the defeat of death, and this verse is where that hope is stated most boldly before the New Testament.

words.note: Bala, to swallow up. The word is used of the earth swallowing Korah (Numbers 16:32) and of the great fish swallowing Jonah (Jonah 1:17). In verses 7 and 8 the LORD swallows the shroud over the nations and then death, turning death's own greedy appetite against it.

Mavet, death. In the Old Testament death is an enemy and a power, not a natural friend. Verse 8 promises that God will swallow it up forever, the text Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 15:54 when he describes the resurrection.

Qavah, to wait for, to hope. The root may be related to a word for a cord stretched taut. In verse 9 it appears twice, and it describes expectant trust rather than passive delay. Those who sing at the feast are those who kept hoping in God before they saw his rescue.

christ: The New Testament quotes this chapter directly. Paul, describing the resurrection of the body, says that when the perishable puts on the imperishable the saying will come true, "Death has been swallowed up in victory" (1 Corinthians 15:54, drawing on verse 8). Revelation twice takes up the promise that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 7:17; 21:4). Jesus spoke of many coming from east and west to recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 8:11), and the Lord's Supper points ahead to the day he will drink the fruit of the vine new in the kingdom of God (Mark 14:25). Christians read the resurrection of Jesus as the first fulfillment of this chapter: in him death was swallowed up, and the feast for all peoples was opened.

hard.q: Does this chapter really teach the end of death, or is it a poetic way of describing national restoration?
hard.a:
Interpreters differ. Some read verse 8 as a vivid metaphor for the end of Israel's national humiliation, the death of exile and defeat, in the way Ezekiel 37 uses dry bones to picture Israel's return. Others argue that the language goes beyond metaphor: the tears are wiped from every face, the covering over all nations is removed, and death is swallowed forever, which suggests the literal end of death. Many scholars see this chapter, together with 26:19 and Daniel 12:2, as a key stage in the Old Testament's growing hope of resurrection.

These readings need not exclude each other. The prophet may have seen Israel's restoration as the first part of a larger undoing of death. The New Testament, for its part, reads verse 8 as a promise about bodily resurrection, and the church confesses that promise on the ground of Christ's own resurrection.

questions: The LORD's feast is for all peoples, with the best food and wine. What does this picture suggest about how God regards the physical world and human joy?
Verse 4 calls God a refuge for the poor and needy. How does the chapter connect God's care for the vulnerable with his final defeat of death?
The redeemed say, "we have waited for Him." What makes waiting for God hard, and what in this chapter makes it worthwhile?
